worksheets.title: Complementary Events, Venn Diagrams and Two-Way Tables

fluency_questions.prompt: Use the complementary event rule $\Pr(A') = 1 - \Pr(A)$ to find $\Pr(A')$ for each event:
In a Venn diagram with $\xi = 50$ students, $n(A) = 28$, $n(B) = 22$, and $n(A \cap B) = 12$. Find:
A letter is chosen at random from the $10$ letters of the word $\text{AUSTRALIAN}$. Find the probability of selecting:

parts.label: b
parts.question: A vowel ($\text{A, E, I, O, U}$)

application_questions.question: In a group of $60$ tourists visiting Phillip Island, $38$ visit the Penguin Parade ($P$), $29$ visit the Koala Conservation Reserve ($K$), and $8$ visit neither attraction. Find (a) how many tourists visit BOTH attractions and (b) the probability that a randomly selected tourist visits the Penguin Parade only.

A $2 \times 2$ two-way table records $120$ Year 8 students who either walk to school ($W$) or take public transport ($W'$), and whether they wear a blazer ($B$) or jumper ($B'$): $n(W \cap B) = 28$, $n(W) = 45$, and $n(B) = 72$. Complete the table counts and find $\Pr(W' \cap B')$.

A spinner with $4$ equal sectors numbered $1, 2, 3, 4$ is spun twice ($16$ equally likely outcomes). Find the probability that (a) the sum of the two spins is $6$, and (b) at least one of the two spins is a $4$.

A box of chocolates contains $6$ dark chocolates and $4$ milk chocolates ($10$ in total). Two chocolates are eaten one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that both chocolates are dark.

reasoning_questions.question: For two events $A$ and $B$, $\Pr(A) = 0.45$ and $\Pr(B) = 0.35$. What is the maximum possible value of $\Pr(A \cup B)$ (when $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive), and what is the minimum possible value of $\Pr(A \cup B)$ (when $B$ is entirely inside $A$)?
reasoning_questions.answer: Maximum $= 0.45 + 0.35 = 0.80$ (when $\Pr(A \cap B) = 0$); Minimum $= 0.45$ (when $B \subseteq A$ so $\Pr(A \cap B) = 0.35$).

reasoning_questions.question: Three fair coins are tossed simultaneously ($8$ equally likely outcomes). Explain why $\Pr(\text{at least one Head and at least one Tail}) = 1 - \Pr(\text{HHH}) - \Pr(\text{TTT}) = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
reasoning_questions.answer: Only $2$ of the $8$ outcomes fail to have both a Head and a Tail ($\text{HHH}$ and $\text{TTT}$), leaving $8 - 2 = 6$ favourable outcomes: $\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
